query: A TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy has been reported in a single-phase BCC, dendritic state, with a yield strength of about 800 MPa and roughly 40% strain under lower-temperature testing, but at 1273 K it retains only 330 MPa yield strength and 423 MPa compressive strength at 30% strain. For its use as an intermediate layer that transfers heat between W and CuCrZr while preserving structural integrity, what single intervention could overcome this loss of strength at elevated temperature? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the reported baseline, define the applicable thermal and mechanical boundary conditions, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying with Si can enhance the high-temperature strength of TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy by forming silicide phases that strengthen the matrix and improve oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy in a single-phase BCC, dendritic state
generation.mechanism: Solid solution strengthening and sluggish diffusion effects, as well as improved oxidation resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced high-temperature strength and improved oxidation resistance
generation.baseline: TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy without Si microalloying
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 300-1273 K, strain rate: 1.0 × 10−3 s−1
generation.uncertainty: Optimal Si content and processing conditions for maximizing high-temperature strength and oxidation resistance

falsification_experiment.design: High-temperature compression testing of TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy with and without Si microalloying
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yield strength and compressive strength of the Si-microalloyed alloy are not significantly higher than those of the non-microalloyed alloy at 1273 K, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Among notable RHEA systems, the NbMoTaW and VNbMoTaW alloys demonstrate exceptional high-temperature mechanical performance, maintaining compressive strengths exceeding 400 MPa at 1600 °C [,,]. Compared to the significant yield strength reduction (>40%) observed in conventional high-temperature alloys from room temperature to 600 °C, RHEAs exhibit a much smaller strength degradation of only 20–40%, owing to their unique solid solution strengthening and sluggish diffusion effects [,,]. It should be noted that RHEAs lack sufficient oxidation resistance at elevated temperatures [,,], which limits their prospects for long-term use in practical applications. Consequently, significant efforts have been dedicated to identifying effective approaches to enhance the high-temperature oxidation performance of RHEAs [,,,,]. Among various technological approaches, microalloying has emerged as an effective strategy to balance the comprehensive properties of alloys. Lu et al. In this investigation, we employ vacuum induction levitation melting (VILM)—an advanced processing technique offering distinct advantages over conventional vacuum arc melting. The VILM method enables superior homogenization of high-melting-point alloys (>2000 °C) while facilitating rapid volatilization of high-vapor-pressure impurities, thereby enhancing ductility through purity control. Utilizing this technique, we fabricated NbMoTaWSix (x = 0, 0.25, and 0.5) RHEAs with homogenized microstructures and systematically evaluated their phase evolution, mechanical properties, and high-temperature performance (including oxidation and ablation resistance). This comprehensive study provides fundamental insights into the microalloying mechanisms of Si in RHEAs, while establishing a framework for designing next-generation ultrahigh-temperature alloys through strategic phase engineering.
